mcqs.question: A codebase organized as `components/`, `hooks/`, `styles/` folders starts to hurt once the app grows large. What's the core problem feature-based structure fixes?
options: Adding or deleting a feature requires touching several scattered type-based folders instead of one feature folder
Type-based folders are slower for the bundler to parse
Feature-based structure eliminates the need for a shared design system
Type-based folders cannot contain TypeScript files
mcqs.explanation: Grouping by kind scatters one feature's files across several folders, so adding or removing a feature means hunting through all of them; feature-based folders keep a feature's components, hooks, and styles together so deleting it is deleting one directory. Bundler speed and file-type support aren't the actual issue.

mcqs.question: A shared `Button` component in the design-system layer imports a helper from the checkout feature module. Why is this specifically a problem?
options: It violates the dependency-direction rule, coupling the design system's release cadence to one feature and blocking independent releases
It's only a style issue, since imports don't affect runtime behavior
It's fine as long as the checkout module also imports something from Button
It only matters if the app uses a monorepo
mcqs.explanation: Dependencies should only point inward — app shell to features to design system — never the reverse; a design-system component depending on a feature ties its release to that feature and breaks independent testing/release. This has nothing to do with whether the repo is a monorepo, and a two-way import would make the coupling worse, not acceptable.

mcqs.question: A `Card` component has grown five independent boolean props (`isPrimary`, `hasHeader`, `isCompact`, `isDanger`, `showFooter`). What's the better long-term API shape?
options: A single `variant` prop for mutually exclusive states, plus slot-based composition (`header`/`children`/`footer`) instead of visibility flags
Combine all five booleans into one object prop with the same five keys
Split `Card` into five separate components, one per boolean
Leave it as is — booleans are the simplest prop type to type-check
mcqs.explanation: Independent booleans produce untested, unintended combinations as they multiply; a variant prop scales cleanly for mutually-exclusive states, and slots let consumers compose content instead of toggling visibility flags. Bundling the same booleans into an object doesn't remove the combinatorial problem, and five separate components duplicates the shared behavior they all need.

mcqs.question: An org has many loosely-coupled teams that want fully independent release cadences and their own tooling choices. Which repo strategy fits better, and what's the trade-off?
options: Monorepo — it guarantees every team uses the same build tool
Polyrepo — teams keep autonomy over tooling and release timing, at the cost of slower, less-atomic cross-cutting changes
Monorepo — it's strictly superior once a company has more than two teams
Polyrepo — it removes the need for semantic versioning entirely
mcqs.explanation: Polyrepo trades atomic, CI-caught cross-package changes for genuine team autonomy over tooling and release cadence — exactly what loosely-coupled teams want. A monorepo doesn't force identical tooling by itself, isn't universally superior, and polyrepo actually needs semver more, not less, since packages are consumed externally.

mcqs.question: A design system needs to remove a prop that changes a component's meaning for existing consumers. What does mature versioning practice add beyond a changelog entry?
options: Nothing — a changelog entry is sufficient for any breaking change
A major version bump paired with a codemod and a deprecation window, so consumers can migrate automatically instead of being broken outright
Publishing the change as a patch release so it reaches consumers faster
Removing the prop silently, since documentation should already cover it
mcqs.explanation: A breaking change needs a major bump plus tooling to migrate consumers safely — a codemod for automated find-and-replace and a deprecation window so old usage still works with a warning before final removal. A bare changelog, a patch release, or a silent removal all leave consumers broken with no migration path, which is exactly what causes teams to pin an old version forever.

mcqs.question: Team B asks the design-system owners to add `isCompactForCheckoutV2` to the shared `Button` for one screen. What should the owning team do instead, per the pattern this pitfall describes?
options: Add the prop as requested, since refusing slows down team B's delivery
Reject all customization requests from consuming teams permanently

Offer a general composition primitive (slot, className escape hatch, or a real documented variant) instead of a single-consumer-named flag, reserving a new variant for requests that recur across teams
Ask team B to fork the component into their own feature folder
mcqs.explanation: The fix is pushing toward composition primitives or a genuinely reusable variant rather than a flag named after one team's screen, reserving new variants for patterns that recur across multiple consumers. Rubber-stamping every request recreates the boolean-soup problem, blanket rejection just pushes teams to fork anyway, and forking loses the whole point of a shared component.
